h1: Which lager style to pick as an Indian brewpub's house beer
title: Choosing a Brewpub House Lager | Craft Beer School
desc: Helles, pils, Czech pale, Vienna or a rice lager: how founders should choose a brewpub's house lager on taste, tank time, cost and Indian drinkers.
teaser: Your house lager will be the beer most guests order. Choose it for your tanks and your customers, not your own favourite.
standfirst: In most Indian brewpubs the lager outsells everything else on the board. That makes the choice of style a business decision as much as a brewing one. Here is how to make it, style by style, with the tank time and the drinker in mind.
sections: Why the house lager carries the business

Walk into almost any brewpub in India and the first question many guests ask is whether there is something light and cold. They grew up on pale lager and that is their reference point. The house lager is the beer that wins over a table where only one person came for craft beer. It is often the volume leader, the one corporate groups order by the tower and the one that pays the rent.

That is why it deserves more thought than any other recipe on your list. Our guide to flagship beer strategy covers the commercial side. Here we focus on the style itself.
The cost of a true lager

Lager ferments cold, typically around 8 to 13 °C, then needs a cold conditioning period before it is ready. Realistically a clean German-style lager takes four to six weeks in tank where an ale takes two to three. In a brewpub with a handful of fermenters, the lager may tie up a tank for twice as long as the beers around it.

Plan your cellar around that. If the lager is your biggest seller and your slowest beer, you may need more than one tank dedicated to it, staggered so one is always ready. Founders who skip this end up with an empty lager tap on a Saturday night, which is the worst possible moment. Our guide to lagering explains why the time cannot simply be cut.

Helles. Pale gold, soft malt, low bitterness, around 4.7 to 5.3% ABV. It is gentle, rounded and very approachable. For a crowd used to mainstream lager it is the easiest step up: familiar in look, better in taste.

German pils. Paler and drier than Helles, with a firm, clean bitterness and floral hop aroma. Brilliant with food and loved by beer enthusiasts, though some first-timers find the bitterness sharper than they expect.

Czech pale lager. Richer malt, a soft but noticeable bitterness from Saaz hops and often a fuller body. A beautiful beer that needs careful brewing; some versions carry a trace of diacetyl that untrained palates may read as a fault.

Vienna lager. Amber, toasty and gently sweet. It sells well as a second lager but is a harder sell as the main one in a hot climate, where guests want something pale.

Adjunct lager. A light lager with rice or maize in the grist. Crisp, very drinkable and closest to what the guest already knows. It is a legitimate style. In an Indian summer it has real appeal.

Look at who walks through your door. A brewpub near tech parks, serving large mixed groups, will sell most to drinkers who want something easy and cold. A Helles or a well-made adjunct lager suits them. A neighbourhood pub with regulars who already explore craft beer can carry a pils with more bitterness. A venue built around food might choose pils for its cut through rich, spicy dishes.

Watch out for one trap. Brewers often want the house lager to show off their skill, so they reach for a hoppy pils or a decoction Czech lager. Those beers are excellent. They are not always what the majority of guests want to drink three of.
Indian conditions that change the answer

Heat and humidity favour pale, crisp, lower-bitterness beers. Many brewpubs also deal with variable municipal or borewell water, so adjust it rather than accept it: soft water suits Helles and pils. Getting there may mean RO treatment and adding salts back. Ingredient supply matters too. Pilsner malt and German or Czech noble hops are imported, so plan stock and storage so the recipe does not change because a shipment ran late.

For most new Indian brewpubs, a Helles is the safest house lager: approachable, food-friendly and impressive enough to show the quality of the brewing. Run a pils or Vienna as a rotating second lager once the cellar can handle it. If your market is very mainstream and the summer long, a carefully made rice lager is not a compromise; it is a good beer for the room.

Whichever style you choose, the real test is consistency. The guest who orders your lager every Friday notices if it changes. Building that consistency into the recipe, the water and the fermentation schedule is the part that takes training.
faqs: How long does a brewpub lager take to make?
A clean German-style lager typically needs four to six weeks from brew day to serving, including cold fermentation and conditioning. That is roughly twice the tank time of most ales.
Is a rice lager a poor choice for a craft brewpub?
No. A well-made adjunct lager is a recognised style and suits hot weather and mainstream drinkers. What matters is brewing it cleanly and consistently.
Can a brewpub make lager without glycol cooling?
Not reliably. Lager fermentation needs controlled cold temperatures. Indian ambient temperatures are far too warm. Plan for jacketed tanks and a properly sized glycol system.
